title: Arrays
description: One- and multi-dimensional arrays, initialization, traversal, copying, and the Arrays utility class.
objectives: Declare, initialize, and traverse one-dimensional arrays
Copy, search, and sort arrays using the Arrays utility class

content.heading: One-Dimensional Arrays
content.body:
An array is a fixed-size, indexed collection of elements of the same type, declared as type[] name = new type[size]; (or type[] name = {v1, v2, v3}; for literal initialization). Once created, an array's length is fixed and available via the .length field (not a method — a common point of confusion for those coming from Java's own .length() on String). Valid indices run from 0 to length - 1; accessing an out-of-range index throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at runtime rather than being caught at compile time.

Arrays are objects in Java (even arrays of primitives), so an array variable is a reference — assigning one array variable to another (int[] b = a;) aliases the same array, exactly like Java's other reference types.

content.heading: Multidimensional Arrays and the Arrays Utility Class
content.body:
A multidimensional array, most commonly two-dimensional, is declared as int[][] grid = new int[rows][cols]; — technically, Java implements this as an array of arrays, so rows can even have different lengths (a 'jagged array'). Traversal typically uses nested loops, often enhanced for-each loops for readability: for (int[] row : grid) { for (int value : row) { ... } }.

The java.util.Arrays utility class provides common operations you'd otherwise write by hand: Arrays.toString(arr) for a readable string representation (printing an array directly shows an unhelpful memory-address-like string, not its contents); Arrays.sort(arr) sorts in place; Arrays.equals(a, b) compares array contents (== only compares references, not contents); Arrays.copyOf(arr, newLength) and Arrays.copyOfRange(arr, from, to) create copies.

content.explanation: Arrays.toString() is needed to print an array's actual contents (printing the array directly would show its type and hash code, not its values). == compares references (false, different objects), while Arrays.equals() compares contents (true).

keyPoints: Array size is fixed at creation and accessed via .length (a field, not a method)
An out-of-range index throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at runtime
Array variables are references — assignment aliases, it doesn't copy
Arrays.toString(), Arrays.sort(), Arrays.equals(), and Arrays.copyOf() cover most common needs
commonMistakes: Printing an array directly (System.out.println(arr)) instead of Arrays.toString(arr)
Using == to compare array contents instead of Arrays.equals()
Off-by-one loop bounds against .length, causing ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
